extracted.intended_audience: advanced high-school mathematical-olympiad contestants and coaches
extracted.subtask_description: Constructing clear, rigorous solutions to high-level mathematical-olympiad problems (geometry, number theory, combinatorics, algebra) including lemmas, claims, and alternative approaches. Emphasis on correct arguments, useful reductions, and insightful remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and prove intermediate claims/lemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: Break the argument into clearly stated Claims/Lemmas and prove each before using them in the main proof (e.g. 'Claim 1. If a = a(i) < a(i+1), then b(i) = 0.'; 'Lemma 1. Assume that a(i) = M := max a; then b(i + k) = 0 for all k = −M, …, M').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label auxiliary results (Claim/Lemma), give short proofs, then apply them to structure the main argument. Use corollaries where convenient. This both clarifies the flow and isolates technical checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use extremal/minimal or maximal element arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose minimal or maximal elements or indices (e.g. 'Let a = mini a(i) and b = mini b(i).' or 'Begin by choosing a maximal rainbow forest F').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume an extremal choice to derive contradictions or deduce forced zeros/structure. This is repeatedly used (sequence problems, combinatorial constructions, maximal forests) to limit possibilities and unlock structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction by replacement preserving properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Modify sequences/objects while preserving the problem's defining property (e.g. replace all copies of M = max a with 1 and show b-harmonicity is preserved: 'Generate a′ by replacing all copies of M ... Then a′ is b-harmonic, and b is a′-harmonic').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such operations to reduce range/complexity (e.g. reduce values to 0/1) while keeping invariants; then analyze the simpler case. Check carefully that the defining relations remain valid for changed entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit symmetry, reflections and geometric transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use symmetry/reflection/affine transforms to map configuration elements and deduce congruences or cyclicity (e.g. reflections in lines C1A1, C1B1 mapping CH to EX; 'Under the symmetry in C1A1, the line CH ... maps to EX').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify symmetries to map hard-to-handle objects to simpler ones, derive equal lengths/angles, and show points lie on common circles. Also note when an affine transform preserves the combinatorial/lattice structure and key inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reformulate problems in another language (graph-theory, algebraic number theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate the problem to a different formalism that makes structure clear (e.g. Problem 3: convert flights/companies to cycles in a graph and define 'rainbow' sets; Problem 6: use multiplicative order ord_q(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good reformulation can turn an awkward original statement into a standard object (forest, cycles, orders modulo primes). State the translation explicitly and prove equivalence before applying standard tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use maximality to force structural constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a maximal object (maximal rainbow forest, side of maximal elementary length) and deduce that certain edges/points must lie in its components or cannot join different components, yielding structural constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that adding any admissible element would contradict maximality; therefore some elements or edges are excluded or forced to lie inside particular components. Useful in combinatorics and geometric extremal steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average/mean-contradiction arguments for sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Use arithmetic mean properties to force equalities/zeros or obtain contradictions (e.g. definition of b-harmonic: a(i) equals average of neighbouring terms; deduce b(i)=0 if a(i) is strict minimum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare an element to the average of nearby terms. If the average must be strictly greater (or smaller) than an extremal chosen value, derive contradictions. Keep track of multiplicities when terms repeat in the average.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction with carefully checked base cases and injectivity arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove statements by induction after establishing small base cases and using injectivity/surjectivity as needed (e.g. Problem 4 proves f(n)=a^n by induction using Step 1 injectivity result and base checks for n=1..5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly list and verify base cases, use established functional properties to make the induction step solid, and use injectivity to conclude uniqueness where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of modular/arithmetic order and multiplicative orders modulo primes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ord_q(2) (multiplicative order) and divisibility properties to construct or exclude prime-factor patterns (e.g. show ord_q(2)=4p for prime factors q of N=2^{2p}+1 and use this to produce strange pairs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute possible orders from congruences, exclude smaller divisors via congruence contradictions, and use factorization identities to ensure existence of required prime factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply geometric area/lattice-point tools (Pick's theorem, elementary lengths, affine transforms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work with lattice polygons using elementary segments/lengths, Pick's formula and affine transforms preserving lattices (e.g. define elementary length(AB), use Pick to get area 1/2 triangles, and apply affine maps to convert parallelograms to unit squares).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce elementary length to count lattice-point spacings, apply Pick's formula to deduce existence/uniqueness of lattice points of area 1/2, and note when affine invariance preserves the key inequality or lattice structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle special and degenerate cases separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly check and treat trivial or degenerate configurations before the general argument (e.g. if Γ has no sloped sides it's a rectangle; treat unbounded regions separately in lattice problem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify easy or exceptional cases early and resolve them; this often simplifies the remainder of the proof and avoids hidden pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give comments/remarks and provide alternative solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: After the main solution, include remarks highlighting stronger conclusions, generalizations, or geometric/algebraic interpretations (e.g. 'the quadrilateral C1KXL is a square', or alternative more 'Euclidean' approach vs 'affine' approach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add short comments pointing out sharper facts, symmetries, or how the argument extends. Present alternate solutions to showcase different techniques and to provide robustness if one method fails.
